sources.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
sources.text: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ D escribed as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. From the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia to the painstaking world-building of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictional take on Florida, players have shared their wide-ranging experiences with the Guardian, revealing what has surprised and challenged them about this long-awaited release – and what this all means for the series’ evolution. Pete Langhelt, 39, from Colchester, pre-ordered GTA VI “as soon as I could”, and has been looking forward to its release for a long time. “Out of my group of friends I’m probably the only one really nerding out about it,” he says. While Pete hasn’t been able to take time from work in the civil service, he’s still clocked “about 10 hours” of gameplay already. “The core of the missions themselves are pretty similar,” he says. “You turn up somewhere, shoot a load of people and escape. But the development of the characters has changed an awful lot. I have enjoyed the dynamic between Jason and Lucia. I never thought you could make comfortable domesticity into an enjoyable side activity in a video game.” Pete has played all the installments of GTA franchise from the first, when he was “probably too young to be playing”. “I think Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favourite Rockstar game going into this, and it seems to have developed the things that I really liked about Red Dead.” The game encourages exploration, he says. “The day and night cycle seems a lot less intense than GTA V, meaning you don’t feel rushed to get things done. I can let Jason take a slow start to the day before taking a slow drive or boat ride to whatever criminal activity needs completing.” His partner is less keen. “She’ll have to put up with me being on the Xbox for the next few weeks,” he says. A 59-year-old MBA retiree from Venice, Florida, was also struck by just how much of the experience revolves around everyday life. He described it as the “most beautiful, real, open-world game that’s ever existed”. “I was surprised that, with about 10-plus hours of play, most of my time has been spent performing mundane tasks like home repair, grocery shopping, personal grooming and trying to open a bank account. The realism is incredible, but perhaps too real,” he said. “It’s as fully realized as a game world could be. I never expected to see anything more fully developed,” he added. Rob Smeraldo, 28, from Dundee, took the day off work yesterday to play the game on his PlayStation 5. “I made sure I had loads of snacks and Domino’s,” he says. And already, Rob believes that “GTA VI must be the greatest game ever made”. “I think the realism and just the detail put into it is absolutely astounding. The shadows, the way the hair moves when people move around … They took their time, but it’s definitely been worth it,” he says. Rob is a longtime GTA fan and wore a GTA VI T-shirt and drank from a GTA mug to mark the occasion. “I purchased the physical copy [of the game] as soon as it became purchasable – I just wanted the memorabilia, you know?” Ella Delancey, 35, of Berkshire has been playing GTA since she was a child. “GTA III is a huge core memory for me. My brother and I were much too young to be playing it and I definitely wouldn’t let my daughter play it now, but at the time we were obsessed.” So far, the social and brand director has been surprised by how much there is to do aside from pushing the story forward. “I’m not very far into it yet, but I’m already struck by the graphics and the sheer depth of what you can do. It’s very violent, obviously, but I play by the rules, which probably makes me a bit boring. I’ve been birdwatching and exploring, and there’s so much to do outside the main story.” There is one thing she is struggling with, however, and that’s Lucia, one of the main protagonists, leaving her child in a cafe and going to prison, only to come out and start committing more crimes. “As a mother, that doesn’t sit comfortably with me. I know it’s a game and you have to suspend your morals to a degree, but that part has given me pause,” she says. “I do think it’s a step forward that you can no longer hire sex workers as in previous games. GTA still has a complicated relationship with misogyny – and it’s far from perfect, but that change feels significant.” While Ella hasn’t taken any time off work to play, she has set aside time on Friday to play or watch her partner play. “It’s so immersive that it doesn’t feel like a chore, and I can see it replacing our usual after-work TV downtime for a little while,” she says. Clint, 36, who works in the music industry in Chicago, describes the game as “truly one of one”, pointing to its unexpectedly domestic moments and the relationship between Jason and Lucia as some of its biggest draws. “The story is just downright cute. I just had my character build an Ikea table with his girlfriend, and loved it. I typically skip some cutscenes, but now I’m rewatching them when I miss something,” he says. Clint says Jason and Lucia’s relationship is particularly significant, describing it as an example of healthy masculinity that could resonate with younger players. “The main character’s relationship is healthy (at least so far, at six hours in – and ‘healthy’ for a GTA game), which I see as such a posit

sources.title: ¿Qué ha perdido ‘GTA 6’ comparado con los Grand Theft Auto anteriores?
sources.text: El hype por GTA 6 ha pagado con creces. Lo nuevo de Rockstar Games debutó en los últimos días con una respuesta inmejorable tanto del público como de la crítica especializada. La espera de 13 años para tener un nuevo Grand Theft Auto ha valido la pena, aunque a los jugadores también les ha llamado la atención la ausencia de algunas características de sus predecesores . Algunas de estas omisiones tienen una explicación totalmente narrativa, mientras que otras responden a una decisión práctica por parte de los desarrolladores. Está claro que GTA 6 es una propuesta con cada detalle cuidado al extremo y que apunta a brindar la experiencia más inmersiva (y realista) en la historia de la saga. Esto también implica que han tenido que enfocarse en la imagen grande y hacer algunas concesiones en beneficio de la historia que plantea GTA 6 . El caso más notorio es que ya no puedes contratar prostitutas , algo que ya formaba parte del ADN de la franquicia. Pero ojo, que esto no responde a que en Rockstar se hayan vuelto mojigatos o les carcoma la conciencia . Desde la compañía explicaron a ShackNews que quitaron dicha función para resaltar el componente crucial del juego, que es la evolución del vínculo entre Jason y Lucía. “ GTA VI es un juego sobre una pareja en una situación complicada: amantes a la fuga. Si bien hemos conservado muchos elementos de entregas anteriores de GTA , todo lo que hemos implementado en esta sexta entrega responde al espíritu de la historia que queríamos contar y a los sistemas de juego que deseábamos ampliar, tales como el sistema de búsqueda policial, la radio, los atracos y el robo de vehículos. Aunque muchos aspectos de títulos anteriores no están presentes en GTA VI , consideramos que los elementos que hemos incluido son necesarios y complementarios para transmitir las sensaciones y motivaciones que queríamos destacar a lo largo de la historia de Jason y Lucía”. Esto no quiere decir que los jugadores estén obligados a cultivar la relación romántica entre Jason y Lucía. GTA 6 les da la libertad a los jugadores de decidir si quieren que los protagonistas sigan juntos o si prefieren que rompan . No obstante, el hilo conductor que se presenta desde el comienzo incluye un objetivo en común que excede a los protagonistas. Así, incluir la opción de contratar prostitutas parece algo innecesario y descartable . Es cierto que las primeras horas de GTA 6 tienen un poco de girlfriend simulator , pero también es una realidad que transitar ese camino paga con creces cuando las cosas dan un giro para lo peor. Sin meternos en spoilers, hay un punto de quiebre en la misión para trabajar con Mattia que pone todo en su lugar. Pero mucho antes de llegar a esa parte, ni recordarás que el juego no te permite contratar prostitutas y matarlas para recuperar tu dinero. GTA 6 está plagado de minijuegos y actividades complementarias. Sin embargo, los jugadores han notado que falta uno que ya era un clásico de la saga Grand Theft Auto y de GTA Online . Nos referimos, claro, a los dardos . Pero no es el único ausente, pues lo nuevo de Rockstar Games tampoco permite jugar a los bolos . Rockstar también ha dado una explicación sobre esto. La firma prefirió dejar de lado algunos minijuegos en GTA 6 porque ya no había tiempo para hacerlos como correspondía . Estas actividades sirven como una extensión de las físicas del juego, algo que se puede ver en las partidas de pool en The Rusty Anchor, y desarrollarlas como correspondía habría demandado una carga todavía mayor sobre el equipo. Después de todo, cada minijuego es un videojuego con vida propia dentro de otro videojuego. “El caso de los dardos es polémico. A veces se oye decir que hay dinero o tiempo ilimitados, pero ni siquiera nosotros disponemos de ello. Por eso, a veces hay que reconocer que no vamos a ser capaces de alcanzar el nivel que consideramos necesario”, explicó Rob Nelson, uno de los jefes de Rockstar North, a VGC .

stories.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust
stories.summary: The post Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust appeared first on Source .

sources.name: Microsoft Source
sources.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust
sources.text: One year ago at Microsoft Ignite, we introduced Frontier Transformation. The premise was simple: technology exists to serve humanity and deliver real business outcomes. Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. Ignite 2026 is the next milestone in this journey as we introduce new innovations that deliver on the promise of all three of these pillars. Our goal is to build a frontier ecosystem , one that lets every organization benefit from progress at the frontier while preserving what makes it unique. “We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large,” said Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, in his opening keynote at Ignite. “For us, that comes down to three things: keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring you have ownership over your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.” Human ambition: AI should serve humanity, not the other way around It starts with the work people are trying to do, which is why we think of Microsoft Copilot as the new operating system for work. New Copilot Workspaces gives people and agents a shared space to work together as a team. Autopilot, a long-running agent, can manage recurring tasks and move projects forward without being prompted at every step, and Copilot Code lets anyone build dashboards, trackers and apps in natural language with enterprise security and governance built in. Together with Office in Copilot, and features like Today, they make up the new Copilot, which is built to translate raw intelligence into real value. Copilot is already driving transformation at scale among our customers. Volkswagen Group is equipping more than 330,000 employees with Copilot and The Estée Lauder Companies has expanded Copilot to more than 14,000 people across its global workforce. Copilot is also connecting to the systems teams rely on most, including Dynamics 365, as well as announcing Salesforce in Copilot , a plugin available in preview with more than 38 pre-built sales skills. Intelligence: Compound your intelligence without giving away your IP Agents are only as effective as the context they work with. Microsoft IQ is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing and reusing the business knowledge apps and agents need. New business plugins let teams package that knowledge into reusable, trusted context, skills and tools that can be shared across the business. Customers are already turning that intelligence into business outcomes. Publicis Groupe is empowering employees to build custom AI skills that combine Microsoft IQ with Publicis’ industry expertise and proprietary data, then test them against real-world client scenarios. The result is faster innovation, quicker decision-making and greater value for clients. In Microsoft Foundry , new continuous improvement tools help customers develop more powerful agents and even train models automatically based on real production signals: optimizing for quality, latency and cost-effectiveness. New models for coding, cyber image and audio are also being introduced, as well as the general availability of Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , a fast, low-cost decision model for tasks like routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control. Trust: Observability at every layer of the stack and for every person As agents move from answering questions to taking action, trust becomes the deciding factor. There should never be a choice between innovation and safety. Microsoft Perception , now generally available, brings together specialized agents to find, defend and remediate vulnerabilities — powered by models including our MAI-Cyber line — to help defenders stop threats at machine speed. Agent 365 Business Analytics gives leaders a clear view of what their AI is costing and what it is delivering, from task success to hours assisted. And Windows is expanding its operating-system-level protection for agents, with more granular containment with Microsoft Execution Containers, built-in agent identity with Entra support and Agent 365 policies enforced on every device, giving IT more control over agent activity in their organizations. Building on its use of Microsoft Defender, Entra and Purview, BNY is exploring capabilities in Project Perception to further strengthen security and governance. These efforts support BNY’s broader AI ambitions, including its collaboration with Microsoft to complete the first agentic negotiation of a U.S. Treasury trade. Infrastructure: A cloud built for AI at global scale Microsoft builds Azure as a single system, co-designing silicon, servers, networking and racks around what we learn running workloads at scale. As agents increasingly work outside the model, from running tools to compiling code, CPUs matter even more. Cobalt 200 virtual machines , generally available today, deliver up to 50% better performance than the previous generation. Cobalt will reach 23 regions by year end and becomes a significant share of new Azure compute capacity in 2027. Azure Catalyst brings Azure and GitHub agentic tools together in one connected experience for modernizing the applications, databases and infrastructure that AI depends on, and hybrid intelligence on Windows lets AI run wherever it makes the most sense, on the device or in the cloud, starting with GitHub Copilot for coding and Copilot for everyday work. Taken together, today’s announcements demonstrate that the organizations that pull ahead in this next phase are the ones that connect intelligence to their people, their data and their processes, with trust built in from the start. That is the frontier ecosystem we are building with our customers and partners. To see it in action, watch the Microsoft Ignite keynote and

stories.title: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models
stories.summary: OpenAI models optimized circuits used in Jalapeño silicon and improved RISC‑V core designs, showing progress in AI-assisted chip design with GPT‑6 Astra.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models
sources.text: OpenAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI. In August, ⁠ we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD. To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips. We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as: In the vector unit , which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage. In the matrix unit , an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block. Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up ⁠ . We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions. We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline. Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads. We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects. We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero. With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both. For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task. At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets. Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of product

stories.title: Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI partner to bring Le Figaro journalism to ChatGPT
stories.summary: Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI partner to bring Le Figaro’s journalism to ChatGPT through summaries and excerpts, with links to original stories.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI partner to bring Le Figaro journalism to ChatGPT
sources.text: The collaboration will make Le Figaro’s journalism discoverable in ChatGPT using summaries and excerpts, including links to underlying stories. Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI announced a strategic partnership ⁠ (opens in a new window) today to help more people discover and engage with Le Figaro’s journalism. The partnership covers current reporting and archive content from Le Figaro and associated publications, spanning news, business, culture and lifestyle. These articles will be discoverable using summaries and excerpts, including links to underlying stories. Le Figaro will retain full editorial independence and control over its journalism. The partnership builds on OpenAI’s work with news organisations around the world to improve the discovery of reliable information, create responsible applications of AI for publishers, and develop new ways for audiences to engage with original reporting. Le Figaro also plans to introduce ChatGPT Enterprise across various teams to support their day-to-day work. It will explore additional uses of OpenAI technology in its workflows and reader services, guided by its AI charter and editorial standards.

stories.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
sources.text: Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation.
